Italy during the 15th century was a country full of intrigue and magnificence. The tumultuous political conditions created the perfect breeding ground for the birth of a new form of government (called Signoria) and the rise of the most ambitious noble families. After having acted in the dark for a long time, the time has finally come for them to take control of the cities and shape Italy’s future. Their stories will go down in history.

In Signorie, you will play the role of a Signore, a Lord of one of the most prestigious families of the Renaissance. One at the time, players choose one die from a common pool. (Twenty dice in five colors are rolled at the beginning of each round.) You place it on your player board (your city) and perform one of the possible actions. The color of the chosen die determines the action, and the number on the die is a discount on the cost of the action.

During a round, each player can perform up to four actions. At the end of the round, if the sum of a player's chosen dice is equal or lower than 13, he can obtain a reward.

The dice mechanism is easy and innovative and gives players a simple, but challenging choice. Money is always tight, so there is a temptation to choose a high valued dice, but that needs to be balanced with obtaining the reward.

[Rating: 1/10] Too much of doing stuff for stuffs sake. This was the beginning of the end of my love of Euros.

[Rating: 1/10] schwanke zwischen 1 (das "Spiel" spottet jeder Beschreibung) und 2 (ich werde es nicht mehr  spielen). habe den Spieltisch nach einigen qualvollen Runden verlassen. völlig abstrakt, der Plan in der Mitte und der eigene Plan bestehen nur aus Symbolen. Man macht halt irgendwelche Aktionen, die die Symbole vorgeben, die aber überhaupt keinen Sinn ergeben.

[Rating: 1/10] What's Your Game? are scammers, don't buy anything from them! (look up Madeira Kickstarter for evidence)

[Rating: 2/10] I've been thinking about this game since I played it last night, and not necessarily in a good way. It's a perfectly fine game, perhaps a little too fussy, with some interesting ideas and decisions. But the theme just utterly kills it for me.   Renaissance Italy, nobles, marrying off daughters, the whole thing is like a hamburger except the buns are white bread and the meat is also white bread. It's exactly the kind of "theme" I can no longer stir myself to care even a little bit about. [Rating: 3/10] Wouldn't play again unless no other choice. Overall, too many things to do and the gender restrictions make it too difficult to do useful things. When an assignment action aligns on the column that does that action anyway, it feels extra bad.

[Rating: 3/10] The map and random house tiles are just bad. Where is the tension? No tiles I need on the map where I need them oh well. . . .  No spots on the board oh well. . . . . Am I missing some thing or is this just a big flaw ?  Don't think I'll play this again.

[Rating: 4/10] Solid game. I felt rearranging the envelope tiles every turn screwed up the flow of the game. I also felt like the game went on a little too long - 1-2 fewer turns would have made this feel much smoother. Again, overall solid but lacking a wow factor.   Update with second play: I again feel like this game is solid. There’s a lot to like here but it’s just overshadowed by other games with more visual appeal, less downtime at four players, and a shorter playtime. Given the time this one takes, I’d just rather play something else.

[Rating: 4/10] Okey, not so much more. To much micro calculations. The game tells you what to do and lacks tension.

[Rating: 4/10] Dull game that plays by the standard engine-building playbook. Spend first half of game building engine (getting additional actions) unleash engine in back half of game. It is obvious that extra books and money actions are required in the first moves of the game. I felt like I was following a script playing. No interaction to speak of (race for initiative and spots, and taking dice only). No decision tension in this one at all as points come from everywhere. Meh.

[Rating: 4/10] Just a mish-mash of a half-dozen random mechanics, like all "Heavy Euros" that have come out in recent times. Signore is actually quite fine. But then again, nothing to distinguish it from the other rocks in the avalanche.
